questions.question: Describe working conditions in early textile mills, and explain the jobs of piecers and scavengers and why owners employed children.
questions.expected_answer: Days of 12 to 14 hours, six days a week, in hot, humid, dusty, noisy mills with oily floors and unguarded machines that caused serious injuries. Discipline was strict, with fines for lateness, talking or spoiled work and beatings for children who fell behind or fell asleep. Piecers walked beside the spinning machines joining broken threads; scavengers crawled under running machines to sweep up cotton waste. Owners employed children because they were paid much less than men, were thought easier to control, and were small enough for these jobs; some were pauper apprentices from workhouses.

questions.question: Describe the dangers of coal mining and the work done by children and women underground before 1842. Why was the Huskar disaster important?
questions.expected_answer: Dangers included explosions of firedamp, suffocation by chokedamp, roof falls, flooding, shaft accidents and coal dust in the lungs. Trappers, sometimes five or six years old, sat alone in the dark opening ventilation doors for twelve hours or more; hurriers pushed or pulled coal tubs through low tunnels, sometimes harnessed with a belt and chain; in Scotland women and girl bearers carried coal up ladders. In 1838 a flood at Huskar Colliery drowned 26 children, the youngest seven; the public shock helped lead to the Children's Employment Commission, whose 1842 report led to the Mines Act.

questions.question: Explain the arguments for and against limiting child labour, and summarise the main provisions of the Factory Act of 1833, the Mines Act of 1842 and the Ten Hours Act of 1847.
questions.expected_answer: For continuing: families needed children's wages; owners argued shorter hours would ruin profits and competitiveness, that work kept children from mischief, and that government should not interfere. Against: reformers such as Oastler, Sadler and Lord Ashley showed evidence of exhaustion, injury, beatings and deformity, compared it to slavery, and workers demanded a ten-hour day. 1833 Factory Act, textile mills: no children under 9; 9 to 13 limited to 9 hours a day; 13 to 18 limited to 12 hours; two hours of schooling a day for under-13s; four inspectors. 1842 Mines Act: no women or girls, or boys under 10, underground; a mines inspector. 1847 Ten Hours Act: women and young people in textile mills limited to 10 hours a day.
